title_clean: Q&A 2: Margins, MTM vs Option Margin, Expiry Settlement
summary: Q&A clarifying mechanics: buy/sell quantities are always equal (TV 'delivery buying' is interpretation); futures settle daily via MTM while option sellers' margin = span + premium value, rising with the option price; NSE uses a 10% risk-free rate in IV; June-2020 hedged margins ~one-third of naked; expiry settlement uses last-half-hour weighted average, not last traded price.
lessons: Futures: daily MTM cash transfer. Options: buyer pays premium once; seller's margin floats with the option's price.
Expiry settlement price is the weighted average of the last half hour - an ITM option can expire worthless despite a favorable last traded price.
Hedged option positions carry roughly one-third the margin of naked shorts (June 2020 regime).
Crowd consensus is dangerous: markets are structured so only the minority profits.

title_clean: CASH vs FUTURES Market - What's Best for INVESTMENT?
summary: Quantified case for taking long-term equity exposure via futures plus a debt collateral stack: ~Rs 7.5 lakh in Bharat Bond/FD earns ~Rs 50k interest while the long futures roll costs ~Rs 30k/year in premium - net ~Rs 10-20k saving vs cash buying; hedging via short call costs only incremental margin (~Rs 50k vs Rs 1.75 lakh); also covers lot-size, rollover and tax trade-offs.
lessons: For large capital, long futures funded by pledged debt instruments beats cash buying: interest income exceeds the cost-of-carry premium.
A short call against a long futures position needs only incremental margin - cash-market holders pay far more to run the same hedge.
Leverage is not inherently gambling: buying with Rs 100 while committing only Rs 20, keeping the rest safe, is capital efficiency.
Futures gains are business income (expenses deductible); cash equity gets 10% LTCG / 15% STCG - pick the instrument with the tax profile you prefer.
